reply: You came second and got asked about first, which can undo an entire good result. They probably meant it as ambition, and it arrived as a verdict. Tell them what it did to you, plainly, not as an argument. Parents often do not notice they have skipped straight past the congratulations until somebody points it out.[CHIPS]What to say|Tell me more|Something else[/CHIPS]

prompt: my friends all got into the same section and i am in another one and break is not enough time
reply: That is a genuine change to a friendship, not you overreacting. Break-only friendships thin out unless somebody protects them. Fix something outside school: one call on sundays, one shared game, anything with a repeat. Meanwhile, give your own section a proper chance, because sitting near the same people daily does most of the work.[CHIPS]Ideas to try|Tell me more|Something else[/CHIPS]

prompt: i am always the one who organises everything and i think if i stopped nothing would happen
reply: You might be right, and that realisation is a lonely one. Organisers usually get taken for granted rather than disliked. Try handing one thing over explicitly, as in, you pick the place this time, instead of stepping back silently and waiting to be missed. If nobody picks it up, that tells you something worth knowing.[CHIPS]Tell me more|How to hand over|Something else[/CHIPS]

prompt: a teacher said something sarcastic about my answer and the class laughed and i have not put my hand up since
reply: You have stopped putting your hand up over one throwaway comment, which is a steep price, and teachers do get this wrong. You can tell her afterwards how it landed, or tell your class teacher or a parent if that is easier. Then put your hand up once for something you are certain about, which usually breaks the freeze.[CHIPS]What to say|Tell a parent|Tell me more[/CHIPS]

prompt: i have a big friend group online and almost nobody at school and i cannot tell if that is fine
reply: Online friends are real friends, and they are also not a full substitute for somebody standing next to you at break. Keep both rather than choosing. One in-person thing a week, a club or a walk or a study group, changes the balance without giving anything up. Keep the usual online rules going too: no meeting up, no personal details.[CHIPS]Club ideas|Tell me more|Something else[/CHIPS]

prompt: my parents promised a trip if my results were good and now they say maybe next year
reply: A goalpost moved after you did the work is a fair thing to be annoyed about. Ask them straight whether it is money, timing, or a soft no, because an honest answer is worth more than a maybe you keep hoping on. Then ask for something smaller in its place. That is a reasonable request, not a sulk.[CHIPS]How to ask|Tell me more|Something else[/CHIPS]

prompt: i feel slightly outside every conversation lately and i have started making excuses to skip things
reply: Skipping is a relief in the moment and it narrows things over a term. Being half-outside conversations often comes down to the group rather than to you. Pick one thing you actually enjoy and keep going to that one, even when the excuse is ready. And tell a parent how school is feeling, because this is exactly the kind of thing worth saying out loud at home.[CHIPS]Tell a parent|Where to start|Tell me more[/CHIPS]

prompt: my cousin got a bigger cake and more photos at the joint birthday
reply: You shared the day and got the smaller half of the attention. You are allowed to want a day that is only yours. Ask your parents for one small separate thing, even an hour, and say why it matters to you.[CHIPS]What to ask for|Tell me more|Cake ideas[/CHIPS]

prompt: en frienda naan romba miss panren avan vera school ku poitaan
reply: Friends move and the missing part is just proof it was good. Distance changes how often, not whether. Fix one call a week rather than waiting for it to happen by itself, and tell amma you have been missing him. Say it to someone rather than sitting on it.[CHIPS]Call ideas|Tell me more|Something else[/CHIPS]

prompt: i shared a secret about how sad i was and she told two other people
reply: That is a real breach of trust, and being annoyed about it is the correct response. Tell her plainly that it was not hers to pass on. Then choose your next confidant more carefully, and consider a parent or a teacher for the bigger things.[CHIPS]What to say|Who to trust|Tell me more[/CHIPS]

prompt: everyone clapped for the other team and nobody clapped for us
reply: You played hard and got silence back. The whole game still happened, and you were in it. Clap for your own team on the way home, loudly.[CHIPS]Tell me more|A cheer please|Something fun[/CHIPS]
